hints: Calculate the gain in kinetic energy using $\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}m(v^2 - u^2)$ with total mass $105\text{ kg}$.
Calculate the work done against resistance using $W_{\text{res}} = F_{\text{res}} \times d$ with $40\text{ N}$ and $50\text{ m}$.
Combine both terms using the work-energy principle: $W_{\text{total}} = \Delta E_k + W_{\text{res}}$.
walkthrough:
Calculate the increase in kinetic energy of the cyclist and bicycle:
$$\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}m(v^2 - u^2) = \frac{1}{2}(105)(10^2 - 5^2) = \frac{1}{2}(105)(75) = 3937.5\text{ J}$$

Calculate the work done against the constant resistance force of $40\text{ N}$ over the $50\text{ m}$ distance:
$$W_{\text{res}} = F_{\text{res}} \times d = 40 \times 50 = 2000\text{ J}$$

Apply the work-energy principle: the total work done by the cyclist supplies both the gain in kinetic energy and the work done against resistance:
$$W_{\text{total}} = \Delta E_k + W_{\text{res}} = 3937.5 + 2000 = 5937.5\text{ J}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
First, find how much kinetic energy the cyclist and bicycle gained. The formula for kinetic energy is $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$:
$$\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}m(v^2 - u^2)$$

Substitute the mass $m = 105\text{ kg}$, initial speed $u = 5\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and final speed $v = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$:
$$\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2} \times 105 \times (10^2 - 5^2) = \frac{1}{2} \times 105 \times (100 - 25) = \frac{1}{2} \times 105 \times 75 = 3937.5\text{ J}$$

Next, calculate the work done against the constant resistance force ($40\text{ N}$) over the distance ($50\text{ m}$) using $\text{Work} = \text{Force} \times \text{distance}$:
$$W_{\text{resistance}} = 40 \times 50 = 2000\text{ J}$$

Apply the work-energy principle: the total work done by the cyclist must supply both the gain in kinetic energy and overcome resistance:
$$W_{\text{total}} = \Delta E_k + W_{\text{resistance}}$$

Add the two energy values together to find the final answer:
$$W_{\text{total}} = 3937.5 + 2000 = 5937.5\text{ J}$$
